solution.concept_anchor: Chhau collective inscription — rare UNESCO practice and variant distinctions

statement_analysis.statement: The simultaneous inscription of all three Chhau variants as a single collective entry by UNESCO in 2010 is considered an unusual practice in UNESCO's inscription history.
statement_analysis.reason: UNESCO typically inscribes individual cultural expressions; inscribing multiple regional variants of the same art form as one collective entry is a rare practice, explicitly noted in Chhau's case.

statement_analysis.statement: Among the three Chhau variants, only the Seraikella variant is associated with the tradition of elaborate mask-making, while both Mayurbhanj and Purulia are maskless forms.
statement_analysis.reason: Both Seraikella AND Purulia Chhau use masks; only Mayurbhanj Chhau is maskless. This is among the most common misconceptions about Chhau.

statement_analysis.statement: Charida village, the primary centre of Chhau mask-making, is located in Purulia district of West Bengal and has become associated with GI tag discussions for this traditional craft.
statement_analysis.reason: Charida is in Purulia district, WB, and its mask-making craft has been associated with GI tag relevance — both facts are accurate.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know Statements 1 and 3 are correct but are uncertain about Statement 2 (not sure if Purulia also uses masks) may accept Statement 2 and select option (d) 'all three' without verifying the mask-usage fact.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Collective inscription of all three variants as one entry in 2010 is documented as rare in UNESCO practice — Statement 1 is correct.
Verify Statement 2: Purulia Chhau uses masks — the claim that 'only Seraikella' uses masks is false; both Seraikella AND Purulia are masked variants — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: Charida in Purulia district, WB, and its GI tag association are confirmed — Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 applies a scope-extension trap by using 'only Seraikella' to describe mask usage. Students who associate Seraikella with 'royal patronage and masks' as its distinguishing features may accept that Seraikella is the sole masked variant, forgetting Purulia's equally important mask tradition. This is an 'only/exclusive' qualifier trap — the most dangerous pattern in UPSC multi-statement questions.
solution.final_explanation:
Combining UNESCO inscription knowledge with variant-level mask usage is a cross-concept trap.

• Statement 1 — Correct: UNESCO's collective inscription of all three Chhau variants under one entry is explicitly noted as uncommon in UNESCO's records, as most inscriptions are for a single cultural expression or community.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Both Purulia and Seraikella Chhau use masks. Mayurbhanj Chhau is the sole maskless variant. The 'only Seraikella' qualifier makes this statement false.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Charida village is in Purulia district, West Bengal. Its artisan community has made Chhau masks across generations, and the craft's distinctiveness has prompted GI tag discussions.

Value Addition:
• GI (Geographical Indication) tags protect traditional crafts and agricultural products linked to specific geographic locations — Charida masks would qualify if formally tagged.
• The UNESCO collective inscription method for Chhau reflects the shared heritage argument — all three variants share the same cultural ecology.
• Mayurbhanj's maskless tradition is the single most-tested differentiator in exam questions about Chhau variants.

solution.final_explanation:
Costume and musical instrument knowledge must be paired precisely across Chhau variants.

• Option (a): Correctly matched — Purulia Chhau is the most visually flamboyant variant, with elaborate costumes and ornamentation. Mahuri, a double-reed wind instrument, is a confirmed core instrument of the Chhau musical ensemble.
• Option (b): Incorrectly matched — Shehnai is used across Chhau variants, not exclusively in Seraikella performances. Attributing it to Seraikella alone is an incorrect restriction.
• Option (c): Incorrectly matched — The most ornate and flamboyant costumes belong to Purulia Chhau, not Mayurbhanj. Mayurbhanj has more restrained costumes; its expressive tool is facial expression, not costume extravagance.
• Option (d): Incorrectly matched — Dhumsa is a large kettledrum, not a wind instrument. Attributing elaborate vocal compositions to Chhau is also incorrect — Chhau has no vocal component during performance.

Value Addition:
• Mukut (crown) worn by Chhau performers can weigh several kilograms and requires specific physical training to wear during acrobatic sequences.
• The Mahuri is analogous in function to the nagaswaram in South Indian music — both are outdoor processional/performance double-reed instruments.
• Costume-making for Chhau, like mask-making, involves local artisan communities and is part of the broader craft ecosystem.

Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with respect to the visual and musical dimensions of Chhau dance?

(a) Purulia Chhau — characterised by the most visually flamboyant costumes among the three variants; Mahuri — a double-reed wind instrument forming part of the Chhau musical ensemble
(b) Seraikella Chhau — the only variant in which the Shehnai is used as an accompaniment instrument, distinguishing its musical tradition from Purulia and Mayurbhanj
(c) Mayurbhanj Chhau — employs the most ornate crown (mukut) ornamentation as the primary visual communication device, compensating for the absence of masks
(d) Dhumsa — a double-reed wind instrument that provides melodic accompaniment to elaborate vocal compositions in Chhau performances
